summary: Pupils aged 11–12 learn the periodic table as an organisation-by-pattern system whose power is PREDICTION, not memorisation. They discover periodicity by putting element cards in order (atomic weight as Mendeleev did, or atomic number as in the modern table) and starting new rows so similar properties line up until the repeating pattern emerges, use position (group/period) to predict properties and relative reactivity, and understand Mendeleev's historical insight of leaving gaps and predicting undiscovered elements. Core distinctions: groups (columns, similar chemistry; in the main groups, the same number of outer-shell electrons, with helium the exception in Group 0) versus periods (rows), and metals (left/centre) versus non-metals (upper right, plus hydrogen).
misconceptions: The periodic table is an arbitrary chart to memorise rather than an ordered predictive system.
Rows (periods) share properties, confusing them with groups (columns).
The table is ordered by atomic MASS in all cases (Mendeleev's a few anomalies; modern order is atomic number).
All metals are equally reactive (missing the group/position trends).
Elements were placed by discovery date rather than by properties.

activities.title: Become Mendeleev: sort element cards until the pattern snaps into place
steps: Receive a shuffled set of element cards, each showing the element's atomic weight (or atomic number) and a few properties (e.g. reactivity, metal/non-metal, how it bonds).
Put the cards in order of atomic weight (or atomic number), starting a new row whenever properties begin to repeat, so that similar elements line up into columns.
Notice the moment when rows and columns align and a repeating pattern (periodicity) emerges from your own sorting rather than being handed to you.
Encounter a gap — one square that stays empty — and PREDICT the missing element's properties from its neighbours above, below, and beside it.
Commit to your prediction, then reveal the real element Mendeleev foretold and compare it against what you predicted.
Use group and period highlighters to trace Group 1 reactivity climbing down the column and Group 0 sitting inert, then tap any element to read its property panel.
activities.insight: The periodic table is a predictive law, not a chart to memorise: arranging elements so repeating property patterns fall into columns (the modern table orders by atomic number; Mendeleev ordered largely by atomic weight) means an element's POSITION lets you predict its properties and reactivity. It is this pattern-reasoning — not any particular ordering basis — that let Mendeleev leave gaps and foretell undiscovered elements.

activities.title: Tap-a-group reference table: reveal shared trends
steps: Use a tappable periodic table where tapping a group highlights all its members and reveals their shared chemical trend.
Tap a group (e.g. Group 1) to see every member highlighted, then read the shared property that unites the column.
Compare tapping down a GROUP (column) against tracing across a PERIOD (row) to feel how the two directions differ.

Locate metals, non-metals and metalloids and notice they occupy a pattern (metals left/centre, non-metals upper-right, metalloids along the dividing staircase, with hydrogen a non-metal exception at top left), not scattered positions.
activities.insight: Column-mates (a group) share chemical behaviour because they share the same number of outer-shell electrons, and tapping a group makes this shared attribute visible at a glance; this serves as an ongoing reference once the arrange-and-predict discovery has established WHY the table is powerful.

activities.title: Predict-Observe-Explain: Group 1 reactivity down the column
steps: Watch a short clip or records of lithium reacting with water.
Before observing, PREDICT what sodium (the next element down Group 1) will do and state WHY, referring to the group pattern.
Observe sodium's reaction and compare it with your prediction.
Explain the result: elements lower in Group 1 react more vigorously, and say how position in the table let you predict this.
Extend: without looking it up, predict how rubidium (the element below potassium in Group 1) would react with water, and give your reason before seeing any evidence.
activities.insight: Reading the group pattern lets you predict reactivity before observing: a pupil who sees the table as a mere list cannot predict, while one who reads the Group 1 trend predicts a more vigorous reaction further down the column — the stated reason is the diagnostic part.

activities.title: Explain the layout: why these elements share a column
steps: Consider that lithium, sodium and potassium sit in the same COLUMN (Group 1) but are not next to each other in the element counting order.
Explain why the table puts them together in one column — what they share and why that is more useful than listing elements in order.
State explicitly the difference between going DOWN a group and going ACROSS a period.
Say why Mendeleev left empty spaces instead of filling positions in order, and why those gaps mattered.
Describe where metals and non-metals are found — in a pattern, not scattered.
activities.insight: Elements in the same group share chemical properties because they have the same number of outer-shell electrons; ordering by atomic number arranges the table so these repeating patterns line up in columns, which is what makes it predictive rather than a mere list — and why Mendeleev's gaps-and-predictions were a scientific triumph.

activities.title: Optional enrichment: interview Mendeleev
steps: Take part in an in-role conversation interviewing Mendeleev about his table.
Ask why he trusted the pattern enough to leave gaps rather than simply placing the next-heaviest known element in every position.
Draw out how he predicted the properties of elements not yet discovered, and how confirmation later vindicated him.
activities.insight: Mendeleev's daring was spotting a property pattern and trusting it enough to predict undiscovered elements — history that dramatises why the periodic law is a genuine predictive theory, not a lookup chart.

checkQuestion: Lithium, sodium and potassium all sit in the same COLUMN (Group 1) of the periodic table. They aren't next to each other in the counting order of the elements. Why does the table put them together in one column — what do they share, and why is that more useful than just listing elements in order?
checkAnswer: Elements in the same group/column have SIMILAR CHEMICAL PROPERTIES (Group 1 metals all react vigorously with water, form similar compounds) because they have the same number of outer-shell electrons. The table is arranged so that ordering by atomic number makes these repeating patterns line up in columns — that's what makes it predictive, not just a list. Full marks link 'same group = similar properties' to the arrangement.
